newsitem.title: CHILE: Wisconsin governor sees no fast-track till mid-'97.
newsitem.headline: Wisconsin governor sees no fast-track till mid-'97.

text.p: The Republican governor of Wisconsin said he saw no chance of the Republican-controlled Congress approving fast-track powers for U.S. trade negotiators until mid-1997, if ever.

Gov. Tommy Thompson, visiting perennial NAFTA candidate Chile, said he wanted to promote business and investment ties between his Midwestern state and Chile's booming economy, the fastest-growing in the Americas. But he said Chile's entrance into the North American Free Trade Agreement, which would lower trade and investment barriers between the U.S. and Chile, would likely stay bottled up in Congress for now.
Only in mid-1997 would Congress vote on fast-track legislation, he said. If passed, fast-track would clear the way for detailed negotiations for Chile to become NAFTA's fourth member.

"I think you're being overly optimistic," Thompson said, asked about whether fast-track could be approved by April. "I don't see fast-track authority passing any time until middle-to-late (U.S.) summer, if it passes then."

"I personally am a strong supporter of it and as a Republican governor will do everything I possibly can to lobby Congress to give fast-track authority to get Chile into NAFTA," Thompson told a news conference after meeting Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat.
"I was pushing the minister to make sure that Chile is enthusiastically pushing Congress and the president to push forward on the inclusion of Chile in NAFTA," said Thompson.
Fast-track would allow U.S. and Chilean negotiators to draw up a trade treaty without fear of it being amended later by Congress.
Chilean officials have said they won't negotiate unless their U.S. counterparts have fast-track.

The Wisconsin group led by Thompson was the latest in a series of delegations from U.S. states with Republican governors hoping to drum up business ties with Chile, whose economy is growing about eight percent a year and attracting heavy foreign investment.
Delegations from Massachusetts, Mississippi and New Jersey have also visited recently, although not all with their governors.
